summary: Defines the addressing architecture of IP version 6, including how addresses are written, the types of addresses, and how they are used. It was replaced by RFC 3513.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number that names one network interface or a group of them. This RFC sets out how those bits are divided, how an address is written in text, and how the leading bits tell a receiving node whether the address means one interface, the nearest of several, or every member of a group.

questions: what is the ipv6 loopback address
what are the three kinds of ipv6 address
subtitle: How IPv6 addresses are built, written down, and told apart from one another.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needed one set of rules that says what an address is, how the bits inside it are laid out, how it is written in text, and how a node tells one kind of address from another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a 128-bit address model with three delivery types (unicast, anycast and multicast), a table of leading-bit format prefixes that name the type, and three conventional text forms including the :: compression of runs of zero bits.
tldr.outcome: The rules let independent implementations agree on which addresses are link-local, which are multicast, and how to parse an address written by someone else. The document was obsoleted by RFC 3513, which carries the same architecture forward.

facts.label: Multicast scope values
facts.value: 1 node-local, 2 link-local, 5 site-local, 8 organization-local, E global

today: RFC 2373 was published in July 1998 as a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3513, which restates the IPv6 addressing architecture and updates parts of it. The document had itself replaced RFC 1884.

sections.title: The IPv6 Addressing Model
sections.content:
An IPv6 address is a 128-bit identifier for an interface or for a set of interfaces. The RFC defines three kinds. A unicast address identifies a single interface, and a packet sent to it is delivered to that interface. An anycast address identifies a set of interfaces, and a packet sent to it is delivered to the one the routing protocols consider nearest. A multicast address also identifies a set of interfaces, and a packet sent to it is delivered to all of them.

IPv6 has no broadcast address. The job a broadcast address would do, reaching every host on a network at once, is done by multicast instead.

Addresses belong to interfaces, not to whole machines. A unicast address refers to one interface, and since each interface belongs to a single node, any of a node's unicast addresses can serve as an identifier for that node. Every interface must have at least one link-local unicast address, and a single interface may carry several addresses of any type or scope. A subnet prefix is associated with one link, and the same link may carry more than one subnet prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number. It can name one network interface, the nearest of several interfaces, or every interface in a group. There is no broadcast address: multicast covers that job. Addresses belong to interfaces rather than to machines, so one machine can have several.

sections.title: Writing Addresses and Prefixes in Text
sections.content:
The preferred text form is x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, where each x is the hexadecimal value of one of the eight 16-bit pieces of the address, for example FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210 or 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A. Leading zeros inside a piece may be left out, but every piece must keep at least one digit.

Because some allocation methods produce long runs of zero bits, a second rule compresses them: :: stands for one or more groups of 16 zero bits and may appear only once in an address. It can compress leading zeros, trailing zeros, or both, so 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A may be written 1080::8:800:200C:417A, and the loopback address 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 as ::1.

A third form helps where IPv4 and IPv6 are mixed: x:x:x:x:x:x:d.d.d.d, with six 16-bit pieces followed by the four decimal octets of an IPv4 address, for example 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:129.144.52.38 or ::13.1.68.3. A prefix is written as an address followed by a slash and a decimal length, such as 12AB::CD30:0:0:0:0/60, where the number counts how many of the leftmost bits form the prefix. The same 60-bit prefix has several legal spellings, but trailing zeros inside a 16-bit piece may not be dropped, so 12AB:0:0:CD3/60 is not a legal way to write it.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address is normally written as eight groups of four hex digits, separated by colons. Runs of zero groups can be shortened to a double colon, and that shortcut may be used only once per address. A prefix adds a slash and a number saying how many leading bits belong to the prefix.

sections.title: Format Prefixes Identify the Address Type
sections.content:
The kind of an address is given by its leading bits. The variable-length field made of those leading bits is called the Format Prefix (FP). The initial allocation reserves 0000 0000 (1/256 of the space) and 0000 0001 (1/256), gives 0000 001 to NSAP allocation and 0000 010 to IPX allocation, assigns 001 (1/8) to aggregatable global unicast addresses, 1111 1110 10 (1/1024) to link-local unicast addresses, 1111 1110 11 (1/1024) to site-local unicast addresses, and 1111 1111 (1/256) to multicast addresses. Everything else is unassigned.

Fifteen percent of the address space is allocated at the start and the remaining 85 percent is reserved for future use, either to expand what already exists or to serve new purposes such as separate locators and identifiers. The allocation supports direct allocation of aggregation addresses, local use addresses and multicast addresses at the same time.

Unicast and multicast addresses are told apart by the high-order octet: a value of FF means multicast, and any other value means unicast. Anycast addresses are taken from the unicast space, so they are not syntactically distinguishable from unicast addresses and a node has to be configured to know that a given unicast address is being used as an anycast address.
sections.plainLanguage: The first few bits of an address say what kind of address it is. That field is called the format prefix. Only a small part of the address space was handed out when IPv6 was designed, and most of the rest was kept free. A leading byte of FF means the address is multicast; anycast addresses look exactly like ordinary unicast addresses.

sections.title: Unicast Addresses and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
The tail of a unicast address holds an interface identifier, which names one interface on a link and must be unique on that link. It is often the same as the interface's link-layer address. In many of the format prefixes the interface identifier is required to be 64 bits in IEEE EUI-64 format, and the universal/local bit (the u bit) must be inverted when it is formed: set to one for global scope, zero for local scope. The inversion is what lets an administrator hand-configure simple local identifiers such as ::1 and ::2 instead of 0200:0:0:1 and 0200:0:0:2.

Two unicast addresses have fixed meanings. The unspecified address 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 must never be assigned to a node: it stands for the absence of an address, for example in the source address of packets an initializing host sends before it has learned its own address, and it must not be used as a destination. The loopback address 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 lets a node send a packet to itself; it may never be assigned to a physical interface, and a packet with that destination must never leave the node or be forwarded by a router.

Two further forms carry an IPv4 address in the low-order 32 bits. The IPv4-compatible IPv6 address is 80 zero bits, then 16 zero bits, then the IPv4 address; nodes that tunnel IPv6 packets over IPv4 routing infrastructure are given these. The IPv4-mapped IPv6 address is 80 zero bits, then FFFF, then the IPv4 address, and is used to represent IPv4-only nodes as IPv6 addresses.

The aggregatable global unicast address divides into a 3-bit format prefix, a 13-bit top-level aggregation identifier, 8 reserved bits, a 24-bit next-level aggregation identifier, a 16-bit site-level aggregation identifier and the 64-bit interface identifier. Local-use unicast addresses come in two sizes: the link-local address is 1111111010, 54 zero bits and a 64-bit interface identifier, used on a single link for tasks such as auto-address configuration and neighbor discovery, and routers must not forward link-local packets to another link; the site-local address is 1111111011, 38 zero bits, a 16-bit subnet identifier and a 64-bit interface identifier, used inside one site, and routers must not forward site-local packets outside that site.
sections.plainLanguage: The end of a unicast address names one interface on the link, and that name has to be unique on that link. Two addresses are fixed: the all-zero address means "I have no address yet", and the loopback address sends a packet back to the machine itself. Two other forms put an old IPv4 address inside an IPv6 one, for hosts that tunnel IPv6 over IPv4 and for IPv4-only hosts.

sections.title: Anycast, Multicast and the Addresses a Node Must Know
sections.content:
An anycast address is assigned to more than one interface, and a packet sent to it is routed to the nearest interface holding it, measured by the routing protocols. Because it comes from the unicast space, a node holding one must be configured to know that it is anycast. Two restrictions apply: an anycast address must not be used as a source address, and it must not be assigned to a host, only to a router. One anycast address is predefined: the Subnet-Router anycast address, which is a subnet prefix followed by fourteen zero bits, so a packet sent to it reaches one router on that subnet. All routers must support it for the subnets where they have interfaces. Each member of an anycast set must be advertised as a separate host route inside the region that contains all of them, and outside that region the address may be aggregated into the advertisement for the covering prefix.

A multicast address is made of a leading byte of 11111111, four flag bits, a four-bit scope and a 112-bit group identifier. In the flags, T = 0 marks a permanently assigned address and T = 1 a transient one. The scope values are 1 for node-local, 2 for link-local, 5 for site-local, 8 for organization-local and E for global; 0 and F are reserved and the rest are unassigned. The meaning of a permanent address does not depend on its scope, so with a group identifier of 101 the address FF01::101 means all NTP servers on the same node, FF02::101 all NTP servers on the same link, FF05::101 all NTP servers at the same site and FF0E::101 all NTP servers in the Internet.

Some multicast addresses are predefined: FF00::0 through FF0F::0 are reserved and never assigned; FF01::1 and FF02::1 are the all-nodes addresses; FF01::2, FF02::2 and FF05::2 are the all-routers addresses; and the solicited-node address FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FFXX:XXXX is computed by appending the low-order 24 bits of a unicast or anycast address to the prefix FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF00::/104. A host must recognize its own link-local address for each interface, its assigned unicast addresses, the loopback address, the all-nodes multicast addresses, the solicited-node address of each address it holds, and the multicast addresses of the groups it belongs to. A router must recognize all of those, plus the Subnet-Router anycast addresses for the interfaces it routes on, any other anycast addresses it is configured with, and the all-routers multicast addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: An anycast address is one that several routers share, and a packet sent to it goes to the closest of them. A multicast address names a group of nodes, and its scope field says how far the packet should travel: the same node, the same link, the same site, the whole Internet. Every node must know a fixed list of addresses as being its own, including its loopback address and the group addresses for all nodes and all routers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section of the RFC is one sentence: IPv6 addressing documents do not have any direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, and authentication of IPv6 packets is defined in a separate document, RFC 1826.

The addressing rules themselves still carry obligations that an implementer has to honour. The unspecified address must not be used as a destination and must never be assigned to a node; the loopback address must never be assigned to a physical interface, and a packet addressed to it must never be forwarded off the node; link-local addresses must not be forwarded to another link and site-local addresses must not be forwarded outside their site; multicast addresses must not be used as source addresses and must not appear in a routing header; and an anycast address must not be used as a source address and may be assigned only to a router.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says little about security, because addressing does not protect packets; that job belongs to a separate authentication document. It does fix strict rules about which addresses may travel how far. Loopback packets stay on the machine, link-local packets stay on the link, and site-local packets stay inside the site.

fields.name: Top-Level Aggregation ID
fields.desc: The top-level aggregation point the address sits under.

fields.name: Next-Level Aggregation ID
fields.desc: The next aggregation level below the top level.

fields.name: Site-Level Aggregation ID
fields.desc: The site that holds the interface.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Names the interface on its link; unique on that link.
A high-order octet of FF marks the address as multicast.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The top three are reserved and must be zero. T = 0 is permanent, T = 1 transient.

fields.name: Scope
fields.desc: 1 node-local, 2 link-local, 5 site-local, 8 organization-local, E global.

fields.name: Group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the multicast group, permanent or transient, within the scope.
